newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid distribution resumes after shelling in Goma.
newsitem.headline: Aid distribution resumes after shelling in Goma.

text.p: Aid workers resumed unloading food aid at a hospital in the Zairean town of Goma on Wednesday after at least one shell crashed into the hospital compound, aid officials said.
They said the shell exploded by Goma Central Hospital as a truck carrying food was being unloaded and two more shells hit in or near the compound but no casualties were reported.
U.N. staff ran for cover and then withdrew the trucks to U.N. refugee agency headquarters in the city centre.

"The second truck has now returned to the hospital and is now offloading but it is a signal of what things could be like if we want to mount a major operation in Goma," said Michelle Quintaglie, a U.N. World Food Programe (WFP) spokeswoman.
She said 10 tonnes of food were delivered to feed 1,000 people in the hospital and others at health centres and orphanages around Goma, which was captured by rebels more than a week ago.
She said the food would go to 850 unaccompanied children, 150 malnourished people and 500 elderly and handicapped.
The food, medical supplies and blankets arrived in Goma from Rwanda on Monday but distribution was delayed until Wednesday by talks between rebels and aid agency officials.
The aid brought by U.N. and independent agencies had been kept at the city's football stadium under rebel guard until agreement between rebel leader Laurent Kabila and U.N. officials.
The shelling erupted after rebels fired at an unidentified twin-propeller light plane flying repeatedly over Goma, saying they suspected it was carrying French troops. It was not apparently hit.
Four mortar bombs or artillery rounds slammed into the foot of Mount Goma shortly after rebels fired towards Mugunga refugee camp to the west from Mount Goma, witnesses said.
WFP officials said 750 tonnes of food were in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi, 150 tonnes of it maize loaded on trucks ready to move across into Goma city.

Aid workers said the arrival of more supplies depended on talks with the rebels and the security situation. They said it was very difficult to assess needs because there was very little information about Mugunga, which was the world's largest refugee camp with some 400,000 residents.
Rebel forces say Mugunga is held by exiled Rwandan troops and militiamen who were responsible for Rwanda's 1994 genocide and are using the refugees as "human shields" against an attack.
